**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 60, Verse 1:**

(p-235) **Surat al-Mumtahanah** (The Woman Being Tested)

Medinan, and its verses number thirteen.

﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a. The reason was that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prepared for the campaign of the Conquest (al-Fath), Hatib wrote to the people of Makkah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended to come against them, so they should take their precautions. He sent it with Sarah, a freedwoman (mawla) of Banu al-Muttalib. Jibril, peace be upon him, then brought the news to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent 'Ali, 'Ammar, Talhah, al-Zubayr, al-Miqdad, and Abu Marthad, and said: "Go until you reach Rawdat Khakh, for there is a riding woman with her a letter from Hatib to the people of Makkah. Take it from her and let her go. If she refuses, strike off her neck." They overtook her there, and she denied having it. 'Ali drew his sword, and they took it from her braids (iqas). Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Hatib and said: "What led you to this?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have not disbelieved since I embraced Islam, nor have I deceived you since I gave you counsel. But I was a man attached to Quraysh without being of them, and I have no kin among them to protect my family. So I wanted to gain a hand (a favor) among them, and I knew that my letter would not avail them anything." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) accepted his truthfulness and accepted his excuse.

﴿You convey to them with affection﴾: meaning, you transmit to them. The particle *bā'* (ب) here is *zā'ida* (superfluous/emphatic), as in the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿and do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. Or the meaning is: you convey to them the reports of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, because of the affection that is between you and them. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of *"do not take"*, or a descriptive clause (*sifah*) for *"allies"*. The pronoun appearing in descriptive words that refer to other than their subject is required only for nouns (*ism*), not for verbs (*fi'l*), or else the clause is a new sentence (*isti'naf*).

﴿And they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth﴾: this is a circumstantial clause from the subject of *"you convey"*. It has been said that it is from the subject of *"do not take"*. It was also read as *"li-ma jaa'akum"* (لِما جاءَكُمْ), meaning: they disbelieved on account of what came to you, i.e., making the very thing that is the cause of faith into a cause of disbelief.

﴿They expel the Messenger and you﴾: that is, from Makkah. This is either a circumstantial clause from the subject of *"disbelieved"*, or a new sentence explaining their disbelief. The present tense form is used to bring the scene vividly before the mind. The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿because you believe in Allah, your Lord﴾ is the reason for the expulsion. In it there is the priority of the addressed over the absent (taghlib al-mukhatab 'ala al-gha'ib), and a shift (iltifat) from the first person to the third person, to signal what necessitates faith, namely divinity and lordship.

(p-236) ﴿If you have gone out in jihad in My way and seeking My good pleasure﴾: this is connected to *"do not take"*, as if it were said: do not befriend My enemies if you are My friends. The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿you confide to them with affection﴾ is a new sentence in the manner of rebuke and reproach, meaning: you confide to them affection, or reports, because of affection.

﴿And I know﴾: that is, while the state is that I know more than you.

﴿what you conceal and what you disclose﴾: and I inform My messenger of what you confide. So what benefit do you have in secrecy? It has been said that *"a'lamu"* (أعلم) is in the present tense, the *bā'* is superfluous, and *"ma"* (ما) is either a relative pronoun or a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*). The priority of concealing over disclosing has already been explained in the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they disclose﴾.

﴿And whoever of you does it﴾: that is, the taking (of enemies as allies).

﴿has indeed strayed from the right way﴾: he has indeed missed the path of truth and rightness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 60, verse 2:

﴿If they overcome you﴾ i.e., if they gain the upper hand over you.

﴿They will be enemies to you﴾ i.e., they will manifest what is in their hearts of enmity and act upon its rulings.

﴿And will stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil﴾ with that which will grieve you, such as killing, capture and reviling.

﴿And they wish that you would disbelieve﴾ i.e., they wish for your apostasy (irtidad). The use of the past tense (sighah al-madi) is to signal the certainty of their desire, even before they overcome you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 60, verse 3:

﴿Your relatives will not benefit you﴾ — "relatives" means your kinship ties (qarabat).

﴿Nor your children﴾ — those whom you befriend, the polytheists, for their sake, and whom you draw near to by defending them (muhamah 'alayhim).

﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ — by bringing benefit or averting harm.

﴿He will separate between you﴾ — this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining why relatives and children will be of no benefit on that day. That is: Allah will separate you from one another by the terror that will overtake you, which compels each of you to flee from the other, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when a man will flee from his brother﴾ [80:34], and so on. Why, then, do you abandon the right of Allah Exalted for the sake of preserving the right of one of such a state? It is also read as "yufsalu" and "yufassalu" in the passive voice, and as "yafsilu" and "yufassilu" in the active voice, where the agent is Allah Exalted, and as "nafsilu" and "nufassilu" with the letter nun.

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ — so He will recompense you for it.

**Abu al-Su'ud's Commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 60, Verse 4**

﴿There has already been for you an excellent example﴾: that is, a praiseworthy trait truly deserving of being followed and taken as a model.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in Abraham and those with him﴾, that is, from among his believing companions, is a second description of "example" (uswah), or it is the predicate of "kana" (was). "Lakum" (for you) is for clarification, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the hidden pronoun in "hasanah" (excellent), or it is a complement (silah) of it, not of "uswah," according to those who do not permit the operation (of a word) after the description.

﴿When they said﴾ is an adverbial phrase (zarf) for the predicate of "kana."

﴿to their people: Indeed, we are free of you﴾: "bura'" is the plural of "bari'" (free from), like "zarif" and "zurafa'." It is also read "bira'" like "zirafa'," and "bura'" like "rukhal," and "bara'" as a description by the verbal noun for emphasis.

﴿and of what you worship other than Allah﴾: that is, of the idols.

﴿We have rejected you﴾: that is, your religion, or your deity, or you and it. So we do not regard your affair or your gods.

﴿And there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever﴾: that is, this is our way with you, which we will not abandon.

﴿until you believe in Allah alone﴾: and abandon what you are upon of polytheism. Then enmity will turn into friendship and hatred into love.

﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you"﴾: this is an exception from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿an excellent example﴾. Abraham's seeking forgiveness for his disbelieving father, upon him be peace, although permissible by reason and by the law because it occurred before it became clear that he was among the people of the Hellfire, as the text states, is nonetheless not something that should be taken as a model at all. What is meant by the model is that which must be followed definitively, since a threat is attached to turning away from it by His saying, exalted is He, which will come: ﴿And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾. Therefore, the exception from the "example" only indicates that it is not obligatory to request faith and forgiveness for an unbeliever whose faith is hoped for, and no sensible person doubts this. As for its impermissibility, the exception gives no evidence for it at all. As for the explanation that his seeking forgiveness for his disbelieving father, upon him be peace, is not something to be taken as a model because it occurred before the prohibition, or because of a promise he had made to him, this is utterly without foundation, since it is based on the assumption that the prohibition covered his seeking forgiveness for him, upon him be peace, and that it indicates he would have been a model had he not been forbidden. Both are clearly invalid, because the object of the prohibition is seeking forgiveness for an unbeliever after his state has become clear. You know that his seeking forgiveness for his father, upon him be peace, occurred before that, definitively, and that what is to be taken as a model is what must be followed, not what is permissible to do in general. The supposition that his seeking forgiveness for him, upon him be peace, occurred after the prohibition, as is understood from the apparent meaning of his saying "or because of a promise he had made to him," has no basis. The direction of the exception toward the promise of seeking forgiveness, rather than toward the seeking of forgiveness itself, is supported by His saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for my father﴾ (the verse), because that was what moved him, upon him be peace, to seek forgiveness. The singling out of this promise for mention, rather than what occurred in Surah Maryam in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord﴾, is because it came in the form of an oath for emphasis. As for making the seeking of forgiveness revolve around it, and making disassociation depend on the clarification of the matter, its verification has already passed in Surah al-Tawbah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I have no power for you against Allah in the least﴾ is part of the excepted speech. Its place is in the accusative, as it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the doer of "I will surely seek forgiveness for you." That is: I seek forgiveness for you, and I have no power except to seek forgiveness. Therefore, the object of the exception is the seeking of forgiveness itself, not its restriction, which in itself is among the traits of good, because it is a display of helplessness and an entrusting of the matter to Allah, exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned back, and to You is the final return﴾ ...etc. is part of what was related from Abraham, peace be upon him, and those with him, of the excellent example. The fronting of the prepositional phrase serves to restrict reliance, turning back, and return to Allah, exalted is He. They said this after open declaration and the breaking of the staff, seeking refuge in Allah, exalted is He, in all their affairs, especially in repelling the disbelievers and sufficing against their evils, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 60, verse 5:

﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve﴾, by empowering them over us so that they afflict us with a punishment we cannot bear.

﴿And forgive us﴾ what has transpired from us of sin (al-'adhab? no: "ma faraṭa minna" meaning what has preceded from us of shortcoming).

Note: The text as given reads: ﴿And forgive us﴾ ma faraṭa minna min al-'adhab, meaning: forgive us what has transpired from us of the punishment.

﴿Our Lord, indeed You are the Mighty﴾ (al-'Aziz), the Victorious who is never humiliated (p-238) whoever seeks refuge in Him, and the hope of one who relies upon Him is never disappointed.

﴿The Wise﴾ (al-Hakim), who does only what contains far-reaching wisdom. The repetition of the address (rabbana) serves to intensify the supplication and the humble entreaty. As for making these two verses an instruction to the believers from Him, exalted is He, and a command to them to rely upon Him, turn to Him in repentance, seek refuge in Him from the trial of the disbelievers, and ask forgiveness for what has transpired from them, as a completion of what He enjoined upon them regarding severing ties between themselves and the disbelievers, then the noble composition does not support it.

﴿Indeed there has been for you in them﴾, i.e., in Abraham and those with him.

﴿a good example﴾. This is a repetition for the sake of emphasis in urging the following (ittisa', taking as one's example) of him, peace be upon him, and for this reason it is introduced with an oath. His words, exalted is He, ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾, are a badal (grammatical substitution, or apposition) for "for you." Its purpose is to make known that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day does not abandon following them, and that abandoning it is one of the indications of not believing in these two, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾, for this is among the things with which disbelievers are threatened.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 60, verse 7:

﴿It may be that Allah will bring about affection between you and those among them with whom you have been at enmity.﴾ That is: from among your polytheist relatives.

﴿Affection﴾ by their agreeing with you in religion. Allah the Exalted promised them this because He saw in them firmness in religion and strictness for the sake of Allah in opposing their fathers, their sons, and all their other relatives, and in cutting off from them entirely, as a way of comforting their hearts. He fulfilled His generous promise when He granted them victory (al-fath), and their people embraced Islam, so the love and mutual closeness that came about between them was fully realized.

﴿And Allah is All-Powerful﴾ That is: exceedingly capable, so He is able to turn hearts, change circumstances, and facilitate the means of affection.

﴿And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ So He forgives those among the polytheists who embraced Islam and shows them mercy. It has also been said: He is All-Forgiving for what you previously committed of allegiance to them, and for what remained in your hearts of the inclination of kinship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 60, verse 8:

﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you on account of religion and do not drive you out of your homes﴾. That is: Allah does not forbid you from showing kindness to these people, for His words ﴿that you be kind to them﴾ are a substitute (badal) for the relative pronoun (al-mawsul).

﴿And deal justly with them﴾: that is, that you give them their due with justice (al-qist), meaning equity (al-'adl).

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾: that is, those who are equitable (al-'adilin). It is narrated that Qutaylah bint 'Abd al-'Uzza came, while still a polytheist, to her daughter Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, bringing gifts. She [Asma'] did not accept them and did not permit her to enter, so this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then commanded her to let her mother enter, to accept from her, to honour her and to treat her well. It was also said: the intended people are Khuza'ah, who had made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they would neither fight him nor assist anyone against him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 60, verse 9:

﴿God only forbids you from those who fought you over religion and expelled you from your homes﴾, and they are the obstinate ones (ʿutuww) of the people of Makkah. (p-239) ﴿And helped others to expel you﴾, and they are the rest of its people.

﴿That you take them as allies﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal, a grammatical substitution in which the replacement is related to the original by a sense of inclusion) from the relative pronoun; that is: God only forbids you from taking them as allies.

﴿And whoever takes them as allies, those are the wrongdoers﴾, because they have placed allegiance (wilaya) in the place of enmity; or, they are the wrongdoers against themselves, by exposing themselves to punishment.

﴿O you who have believed﴾ is an introduction to the ruling concerning those who outwardly profess faith, after the ruling concerning the two groups of disbelievers has been stated.

﴿When there come to you the believing women, emigrating﴾ from among the disbelievers.

﴿Then test them﴾ That is, examine them by means of what most strongly suggests to your assumption that their hearts agree with their tongues in faith.

It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would say to the woman he was testing: "By Allah, besides whom there is no god, you did not leave out of hatred for a husband. By Allah, you did not leave out of desire to move from one land to another. By Allah, you did not leave out seeking worldly gain. By Allah, you did not leave except out of love for Allah and His Messenger." ﴿Allah knows best their faith﴾ because He is the one who has knowledge of what is in their hearts, and this sentence is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD).

﴿Then if you know them﴾ after the testing,

﴿to be believers﴾ with a knowledge that you are able to attain and that your capacity reaches, after the various kinds of inference from signs and proofs, and seeking testimony from indicators and signs, which is the strongest assumption. Calling it "knowledge" is to indicate that it takes the place of knowledge in the obligation to act upon it.

﴿then do not return them to the disbelievers﴾ That is, to their disbelieving husbands, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾. This is a justification for the prohibition against returning them to those men. The repetition is either to emphasize the prohibition, or because the first (negation) is to explain the dissolution of the first marriage and the second is to explain the impermissibility of a new marriage.

﴿And give them what they spent﴾ That is, give their husbands the same as what they had paid to them as dowries. The reason is that the Treaty of Hudaybiyah stipulated that whoever comes to us from among you, we will return him. Subay'ah bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyyah came as a Muslim woman while the Prophet, peace be upon him, was at Hudaybiyah, and her husband, Musafir al-Makhzumi, came after her. It is said that it was Sayfi ibn al-Rahib, who said: "O Muhammad, return my wife to me, for you have stipulated that you would return to us whoever comes to you from us." So this was revealed to clarify that the condition applied only to men and not to women. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made her swear, and she swore, and he gave her husband what he had spent. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) then married her.

﴿And there is no blame upon you in marrying them﴾ since their Islam has come between them and their disbelieving husbands.

﴿when you have given them their compensation﴾ The giving of the dowry was made a condition of marrying them, as an indication that what their husbands were given does not take the place of the dowry.

﴿And do not hold to marriage with disbelieving women﴾ ʿIṣam is the plural of ʿiṣmah, which is what one holds fast to, by means of a contract or a cause. That is: let there be no marital bond between you and polytheistic women. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Whoever has a disbelieving wife in Mecca, she should not be counted among his wives, because the difference of the two abodes has cut off her bond with him. It is related from al-Nakhaʿi (may Allah have mercy on him) that it refers to a Muslim woman who joins the abode of war and then disbelieves. It is related from Mujahid that He commanded them to divorce the women who remained with the disbelievers and to separate from them. It is also read as "wa-la tumassikū" with the doubled sād, and as "la tamassakū" with one of the two tāʾs of tatamassakū elided (p-240).

﴿And ask for what you have spent﴾ from the dowries of your women who have gone over to the disbelievers.

﴿And let them ask for what they spent﴾ from the dowries of their wives who emigrated.

﴿That﴾ which has been mentioned,

﴿is the judgment of Allah.﴾ His words: ﴿He judges among you﴾ are either a new independent sentence, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the judgment of Allah" with the pronoun omitted, meaning: Allah judges it; or it means He has made for you a judge, in an intensified sense. ﴿And Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ He legislates what the far-reaching wisdom requires.

It is related that when this verse was revealed, the believers paid to the polytheist husbands what they had been commanded to pay as dowries of the emigrant women. The polytheists refused to pay anything of the dowries of the disbelieving women to their Muslim husbands. Then there was revealed the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 60, verse 11:

﴿And if something from your wives has escaped you to the disbelievers﴾ That is: it has preceded you and slipped away from you.

﴿something from your wives﴾ That is: any one of your wives. It has also been read in this manner. The placing of "shay'" (thing) in this position is for belittling and for generalizing with completeness, or [it means] "something from the dowries of your wives."

﴿then you were given a turn﴾ That is: your turn came (ʿuqbah, i.e., your turn) to pay the dowry. What was decreed for the Muslims and the disbelievers was likened to this: that these people pay the dowries of those people's wives at one time, and those people pay the dowries of these people's wives at another time, by an arrangement in which they take turns, just as they take turns in riding and other things.

﴿So give to those whose wives have gone the like of what they had spent﴾ from the dowry of the emigrant women whom you married, and do not give it to her disbelieving husband. It was also said: its meaning is: if something escapes you and you obtain from the disbelievers a "ʿuqbā" (recompense), which is the spoils of war, then give in place of what escaped from the spoils. It has also been read as "fa-aʿqabtum" and "fa-ʿaqqabtum" with doubling (tashdid), and "fa-ʿaqabtum" with lightening (takhfif) with the qaf vowelled with a fatha and with a kasra. It was said: all those who joined the polytheists from the wives of the believing emigrants numbered six women: Umm al-Hakam bint Abi Sufyan, Fatimah bint Umayyah, Barwa' bint ʿUqbah, ʿAbdah bint ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, Hind bint Abi Jahl, and Kulthum bint Jarwal.

﴿And fear Allah, in whom you are believers﴾ For faith in Him, exalted is He, necessitates fear of Him, exalted is He.

﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you﴾ means: coming to you to pledge allegiance, intending the pledge. It was revealed on the day of the Conquest (al-Fath). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had finished taking the pledge from the men, he began taking the pledge from the women.

﴿on condition that they will not associate anything with Allah﴾ means: anything at all, or any form of association (shirk).

﴿nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children﴾ is intended to refer to the burying of daughters alive (wad' al-banat). It is also recited as "wa-la yuqattilna" with the shaddah (intensive form of the verb, meaning "nor slaughter/kill repeatedly").

﴿nor bring a slander they have invented between their hands and their feet﴾: a woman would pick up a newborn and say to her husband, "This is my child from you." This was described by the phrase "slander invented between their hands and their feet," because the womb she carries it in is between her hands, and its exit is between her legs.

﴿nor disobey you in what is right﴾ means: in what you command them of what is right and forbid them from what is wrong. The restriction to "what is right" is mentioned even though the Messenger (ﷺ) only commands what is right, in order to alert that obedience to a created being is not permissible in disobedience to the Creator. The singling out of the listed matters for mention concerning them is because they frequently occur among them, although some of them are specific to them.

﴿So accept their pledge﴾ means: upon what has been mentioned and what has not been mentioned, since its matter is clear and its fundamental nature in the pledge is evident, namely prayer, zakat, and the other pillars of religion and the rites of Islam. Restricting their pledge to what has been mentioned, along with their coming, is to urge them to hasten toward it with full desire for it, without any call to them to it.

﴿and ask Allah for forgiveness for them﴾ is an addition to what is implied in the pledge, for it is an expression of the guarantee of reward from Him (ﷺ) in exchange for their fulfilling the matters mentioned.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ means: He is exceedingly forgiving and merciful, so He forgives them and shows them mercy when they fulfil what they pledged.

There is disagreement about the manner in which the Messenger (ﷺ) took the pledge from them on that day. It is narrated that when he (ﷺ) had finished taking the pledge from the men, he sat on al-Safa, with Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) below him, and he (ﷺ) began stipulating the pledge to them while Umar shook hands with them. It is also narrated that he commissioned a woman who stood on al-Safa, and she took the pledge from them. It was said: he called for a vessel of water, dipped his hand into it, and then they dipped their hands in it. It is also narrated that he (ﷺ) took the pledge from them while between his hands and their hands was a cloth of qaṭarī (a type of striped cloth).

The most apparent and well-known view is that which Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "By Allah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never took anything from the women except what Allah the Exalted had commanded, and the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never touched the hand of a woman at all. He would say, when he had taken the pledge from them: 'I have accepted your pledge,' by words alone. When believing women emigrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would test them. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you﴾ until the end of the verse. When they affirmed that by their words, he would say to them: 'Go, for I have accepted your pledge.'"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 60, verse 13:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take as allies a people with whom Allah is angry﴾ They are the general body of disbelievers. It was also said: the Jews, based on what has been related, that it was revealed concerning some of the poor Muslims who used to associate with the Jews in order to obtain some of their fruits.

﴿They have despaired of the Hereafter﴾ because of their disbelief in it, or because of their knowledge that there is no share (khalaq) for them in it, due to their obstinacy towards the Messenger, who is described in the Torah and confirmed by the signs.

﴿as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves﴾ That is: just as those among them who died have despaired of it, because they came to know the reality of the situation and witnessed their deprivation of its everlasting bliss and their being afflicted with its painful punishment. The meaning is: He described them with complete despair of it. It was also said: the meaning is: just as they have despaired that their dead will be resurrected and return to the world alive. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to indicate the cause of their destruction (bi'sihim).

On the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Mumtahanah, the believing men and believing women will be his intercessors on the Day of Resurrection."
